In [[mathematical logic]], specifically [[recursion theory|computability theory]], a [[function (mathematics)|function]]  <math>f: \R \to \R</math> is ''sequentially computable'' if, for every computable [[sequence]]  <math>\{x_i\}_{i=1}^\infty</math> of [[real number]]s, the sequence  <math>\{f(x_i) \}_{i=1}^\infty</math> is also [[computable real number|computable]].

A function <math>f: \R \to \R</math> is ''effectively uniformly continuous'' if there exists a [[primitive recursive function]] <math>d : \N \to \N</math> such that, if <math> |x-y| < 1/d(n)</math>, then <math> |f(x) - f(y)| < 1/n</math>.

A [[real function]] is thus '''computable''' if it is both sequentially computable and effectively uniformly continuous.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Grzegorczyk |first=A. |authorlink=Andrzej Grzegorczyk |title=On the definitions of computable real continuous functions |year=1957 |journal=[[Fundamenta Mathematicae]] |volume=44 |issue=1 |pages=61–77 |url=http://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/fm/fm44/fm4415.pdf |zbl=0079.24801}}</ref>

These definitions can be generalized to functions of several variables as follows: let <math>D</math> be a subset of  <math>\R^n</math>. A function <math>f: D \to \R</math> is ''sequentially computable'' if, for every <math>n</math>-tuple <math>( \{ x_{i \, 1} \}_{i=1}^\infty, \dots, \{ x_{i \, n} \}_{i=1}^\infty)</math> of computable sequences of real numbers such that
:<math>(x_{i \, 1}, \ldots x_{i \, n}) \in D</math>
for all <math>i</math>, the sequence  <math>\{f(x_i) \}_{i=1}^\infty</math> is also computable.
